criteria.description: Correctly differentiates 3e^{2t} and confirms it matches 2x.
Correctly explains why Ce^{2t} works for any C, and why this is consistent with 3e^{2t} being a valid solution (it's just C=3).

solutions.fullSolution:
d/dt[3e^{2t}] = 6e^{2t}. 2x = 2(3e^{2t}) = 6e^{2t}. Match, so the ODE holds.
For x=Ce^{2t}: d/dt[Ce^{2t}]=2Ce^{2t}, and 2x=2Ce^{2t}, match for any C (the constant cancels out of the comparison). The ODE alone doesn't determine C uniquely, since differentiating loses that information; 3e^{2t} is simply the C=3 member of this family, not in conflict with the general family being valid too. An initial condition would pin down the specific C.

criteria.description: Correctly analyzes the x=3 case: decreasing, approaching x=1 without crossing.
Correctly analyzes the x=-1 case: increasing, approaching x=1 without crossing.
Connects both to the general 'stable equilibrium' picture.

solutions.fullSolution:
For x=3>1: xdot=-x+1=-2<0, decreasing, and as x approaches 1 from above, xdot approaches 0, so the decrease slows and x asymptotically approaches 1 without crossing it.
For x=-1<1: xdot=-x+1=2>0, increasing, and as x approaches 1 from below, xdot approaches 0 similarly, approaching 1 from below without overshooting.
Both trajectories flow toward the equilibrium x=1 monotonically from either side: x=1 is a stable equilibrium, everything nearby is pulled toward it, visible directly from the sign of xdot without solving anything.

criteria.description: Correctly applies the chain rule to d/dt[F(x(t))].
Correctly substitutes F'(x)=1/g(x) and xdot=f(t)g(x), showing the g(x) terms cancel to leave f(t).
Correctly integrates both sides to arrive at F(x(t))=integral f(t) dt + C.

solutions.fullSolution:
d/dt[F(x(t))] = F'(x(t)) * xdot(t) (chain rule).
Substitute F'(x)=1/g(x) and xdot=f(t)g(x): d/dt[F(x(t))] = (1/g(x(t))) * f(t)*g(x(t)) = f(t) (the g(x(t)) factors cancel exactly).
So d/dt[F(x(t))] = f(t) holds for all t. Integrating both sides w.r.t. t: F(x(t)) = integral f(t) dt + C, exactly the 'separate and integrate' rule (since F(x) = integral dx/g(x) by definition), now justified rigorously via the ordinary chain rule rather than treating dx/dt as a fraction.
dx/x = t dt. Integrate: ln|x| = t^2/2 + C. x(t) = A*e^{t^2/2}. x(0)=1 gives A=1. x(t)=e^{t^2/2}. x(2)=e^{4/2}=e^2 ~= 7.389. (Verified with SymPy while authoring this module.)

criteria.description: Correctly expands d/dt[mu*x] via the product rule.
Correctly compares terms and derives the requirement mu_dot = mu*p.
Correctly solves this (separable) equation for mu, getting mu(t)=e^{integral p dt}.

solutions.fullSolution:
d/dt[mu(t)x(t)] = mu(t)*xdot(t) + mu_dot(t)*x(t) (product rule).
Compare to mu(t)*xdot(t) + mu(t)*p(t)*x(t) (the left side after multiplying the ODE by mu): the mu*xdot terms already match, so we need mu_dot(t) = mu(t)*p(t) for the x(t) terms to match too.
This is itself separable: dmu/mu = p(t) dt, integrate: ln|mu| = integral p(t) dt, so mu(t) = e^{integral p(t) dt} (taking the integration constant to be 0, since any valid mu works).

p(t)=3, mu(t)=e^{3t}. d/dt[e^{3t}x] = 6e^{3t}. Integrate: e^{3t}x = 2e^{3t}+C, x(t)=2+C*e^{-3t}. x(0)=0: 2+C=0, C=-2. x(t)=2-2e^{-3t}. x(1)=2-2e^{-3} ~= 2-0.0996 ~= 1.900. (Verified with SymPy while authoring this module.)
